clue.text: Power at a young age-describing certain kings?

parts.note: P is the standard abbreviation for power in physics
something done at a young age is done early in life

explanation.surface: A question about power held early in life and how it reflects on certain monarchs.
explanation.walkthrough: Pearly kings and queens are London street traders' charity figures who wear clothes sewn with mother-of-pearl buttons.
explanation.definitionFit: The button-covered costermonger royalty of London are called pearly kings, so the adjective is what describes them.

clue.text: Residents putting a lot of work into city, perhaps

indicators.note: the shortened work is put into the middle of the other word

parts.note: a city is one example of a place

indicators.note: most of the word is used, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: an opus is a musical or literary work

explanation.surface: Locals push a big workload onto their city.
explanation.walkthrough: 'city, perhaps' defines by example: a city is one kind of place. 'a lot of' signals that the work loses its final letter before 'putting into' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: The populace is the whole body of people living in a place, its inhabitants.

clue.text: Insubstantial Cockney man in panto, maybe?

indicators.note: Cockney speakers drop the initial h, so the h of the first word goes

parts.note: a hairy fairy is a burly man dressed as a fairy, a classic pantomime gag

explanation.surface: A flimsy figure: the Cockney bloke playing a part in a Christmas pantomime.
explanation.walkthrough: Pantomime is a British Christmas stage show where men often play women's or fairy roles. 'Cockney' removes the H from HAIRY, leaving AIRY.
explanation.definitionFit: Something airy-fairy is vague and lacking solid substance.

clue.text: Across You should have this before you depart

definitions.text: You should have this before you depart

parts.words: You should have this before you depart
parts.note: departing here means dying: the clue describes the span of years a person is reckoned to live before death

explanation.surface: A reminder to pack something before leaving on a trip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Across' is part of the printed cross-reference to 13 Across, not a clue word. 'Depart' suggests a journey, but it means die.
explanation.definitionFit: Actuaries estimate the number of years a person can expect to live, which they have before death.

clue.text: Maiden speech initially fixes most of time in office

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word speech is taken

parts.note: pins fixes things in place

indicators.note: the final letter of the word is cut off

parts.note: a term is a period in office

explanation.surface: An MP's maiden speech is said to settle most of their tenure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maiden speech' looks like a phrase, but 'Maiden' alone is the definition. 'most of' cuts TERM to TER.
explanation.definitionFit: A maiden in the old sense is an unmarried woman.

clue.text: Skill has newsmen stifling shocked cry

indicators.note: the press smother the cry, so it sits inside them

parts.note: journalists collectively are the press
ow is a cry of pain or shock

explanation.surface: A talent for keeping reporters from yelling in surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: Prowess is great ability or expertise.

clue.text: Across Round follows round here?

parts.note: a round of drinks is bought at the clubhouse bar after a round of golf, so one round follows the other in this spot

explanation.surface: A puzzle about where one round comes after another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Across' is part of the printed cross-reference to 25 Across. A golf course has eighteen holes; golfers call the clubhouse bar the next one.
explanation.definitionFit: Golfers' slang names the clubhouse bar, where players drink after finishing the course.

clue.text: I'm not ill-disposed? Oh, yes, I am!

definitions.text: I'm not ill-disposed? Oh, yes, I am!

indicators.note: disposed badly, so the letters are set out in a new order

explanation.surface: A pantomime-style exchange: someone denies being grumpy, then admits it.
explanation.walkthrough: Timon of Athens is Shakespeare's misanthrope. 'ill-disposed' rearranges the letters of I'M NOT; the reply 'Oh, yes, I am!' is the pantomime call-and-response.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's Athenian turns against all humanity, the very model of a hater of people.

clue.text: Photo problem's studied -certainly, we hear

indicators.note: the words are spoken, giving their sound rather than spelling

parts.note: read, past tense, means studied; aye is an old or Scots yes, meaning certainly

explanation.surface: Someone has examined a photographic flaw and confirms it.
explanation.walkthrough: Past-tense READ is said like RED, and AYE like EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: A camera flash reflecting off the retina makes pupils glow scarlet in pictures.

clue.text: King's weak on giving warning sound

parts.note: K is the chess and card abbreviation for king
lax means slack or weak

explanation.surface: A feeble monarch carries on making an alarm noise.
explanation.definitionFit: A klaxon is a loud electric horn used as an alarm.

clue.text: Wine? Fool's drunk about one case

parts.note: port is a fortified wine

indicators.note: the rearranged letters go around the numeral
a drunk person's word is jumbled, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the fool's letters, the 's being a link
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A sommelier asks about wine as the jester gets drunk over a case of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'drunk' rearranges FOOL to FOLO, and 'about' puts I inside it: FOLIO.
explanation.definitionFit: A portfolio is a flat case for carrying papers or drawings.

clue.text: Traveller never off the rails?

parts.note: no means not at all, never
someone off the rails has gone mad

explanation.surface: A wanderer who has never lost their head.
explanation.definitionFit: A nomad roams from place to place with no fixed home.

clue.text: Down Like Labour scale of swing?

parts.note: the Labour party sits on the political ..., and a lurch is a heavy defeat or a sudden swing, so the party suffers a big electoral swing

explanation.surface: A question about the size of a voting shift against the Labour Party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' is part of the printed cross-reference to 14 Down. Labour is Britain's main left-wing party; a lurch is a sudden lean or swing, and also an old word for a crushing defeat in cribbage.
explanation.definitionFit: To be abandoned in difficulty, with no help, is the idiom's meaning.

clue.text: See 3down
See 12 across
Some hair where beard grows — that's about good, no?

indicators.note: the chin wraps around the other letters

parts.note: a beard grows on the chin

explanation.surface: A remark about stubble: where a beard grows is fine, surely?
explanation.definitionFit: A chignon is a knot or coil of hair worn at the back of the head.

clue.text: snow vehicle

annotationWithheld.why: Held clue 'snow vehicle (6)' is cut short: lowercase start and no wordplay; no scan or reprint gives the rest.

clue.text: Good beat supplied by instrument in part of Wales

parts.note: to lam is to thrash or beat
an organ is a musical instrument

explanation.surface: A Welsh band: a fine rhythm backed by an instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: Glamorgan is a historic county of South Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: Glamorgan is a historic county in the south of the country, home of Cardiff.

clue.text: Craftsman successfully interrupting gibe

indicators.note: the word for success breaks into the taunt

parts.note: a jeer is a taunt or gibe
doing something well is doing it successfully

explanation.surface: An artisan is heckled, but does well breaking up the mockery.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeweller is a skilled worker who makes or repairs gems and ornaments.

clue.text: Double-barrelledness displays it

parts.note: a double-barrelled surname or word shows a short dash joining its two parts, as the clue's own first word does

explanation.surface: A remark about posh two-part surnames.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's first word holds the very mark it describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Compound words and double-barrelled names are joined by this punctuation mark.

clue.text: One cracking up can't use crackers

indicators.note: crackers means crazy, so the letters are scrambled

explanation.surface: Someone losing their mind finds crackers useless.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crackers' sounds like biscuits, but it is the anagram signal on CAN'T USE.
explanation.definitionFit: A nutcase is a person going mad, slang for a lunatic.

clue.text: This writer's Macbeth, say-it's a gas!

parts.note: the setter refers to themselves as me
Macbeth is Thane of Glamis and Cawdor, a Scottish thane

explanation.surface: A setter proudly claims to be Macbeth and laughs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'it's a gas' looks like the slang for great fun, but 'gas' is the literal definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Methane is a flammable hydrocarbon gas, the main component of natural gas.

clue.text: Principality's record containing brief account

indicators.note: the record holds the abbreviation inside it

parts.note: a mono is a single-channel recording
AC is the abbreviation for account

explanation.surface: A small state's archives include a short report.
explanation.definitionFit: Monaco is a tiny sovereign state ruled by a prince on the Riviera.

clue.text: Obscene book a student's brought in to deliver

indicators.note: the letters are placed inside the verb

parts.note: to rid is to free or deliver
L is the learner driver's plate letter, a student

explanation.surface: A trainee carries an indecent book in to hand over.
explanation.definitionFit: Ribald humour is coarse and vulgar.

clue.text: Down Offensive recording carrying a provision against shock

indicators.note: the two words together hold the letter inside

parts.note: insulting means offensive
a tape is a recording

explanation.surface: An abusive tape that warns of a scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Down' is part of the printed cross-reference to 26 Down. 'carrying' places A inside INSULTING after the L.
explanation.definitionFit: This adhesive strip wraps wires to prevent electric shocks.

clue.text: Leave Adriatic resort

definitions.meaning: a Croatian city on the coast

explanation.surface: Departing a seaside town on the Adriatic.
explanation.definitionFit: To split is slang for leave; the Croatian port city on the coast is a holiday destination.

A student enthralled by the German psychologist

indicators.note: held captive inside, so the letter sits in the German article

parts.note: der is a German word for the
L for learner, a student

explanation.surface: A student is captivated by a German psychology lecturer.
explanation.walkthrough: Alfred Adler was the Austrian founder of individual psychology.
explanation.definitionFit: Alfred Adler was an Austrian pioneer of psychology who coined the inferiority complex.

clue.text: Exotic port and heavenly spirit

definitions.meaning: a far-off Russian port on the White Sea

explanation.surface: A foreign harbour and an angel.
explanation.definitionFit: Archangel is the English name of the Russian Arctic seaport; an archangel is a chief angel.

clue.text: Some Europeans tend much to differ

indicators.note: the letters are made to differ from their order, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Citizens of one country are said to be fond of disagreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Natives of the Netherlands are Europeans.

clue.text: Sound of singer is a note

indicators.note: the word is spoken, so its sound gives the answer

parts.note: a tenor is a male singer

explanation.surface: A singer's voice produces a musical note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'note' means a banknote, not music: a tenner is a ten-pound note.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for a ten-pound banknote.
